title: Is the romantic ideal dated?
summary: John asks whether the balcony romance is dated; Rose says many Americans still hold it, and John says Bix's Whiteman solos sound fresh.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Okay. Now, let me ask, let me ask you this. If we make an analogy between his music and a kind of a romantic stock image, would it be fair to say that the romantic image of the two people on the balcony is pretty much a cliche dated image? In other words, we can look back at those 20 movies with Doris Day or whatever and say, well, this is a genre of the 20s. And we can sort of all partake in them and enjoy them because, well, we know that they're of a certain time and place and we enjoy it. But it's dated and a lot of it's corny.
See, I wish it were dated, John, but I really think that a large section of Americans still hold that image.

They probably do. But my point would be that it's been translated in some other way. Oh, very possible. Now, it may, I don't know what a modern analogy to that would be, but I think that all romanticism is taken out. For instance, sexual connotations in those movies were very, it was the dreamy, elusive, very suggestive, subtly suggestive sexuality. No overt sexuality at all. Very subtly suggestive. Oh, of course. Now, today you get the exact opposite. That's true. If there's any less subtle suggestiveness of sex as today in the movies, you know. So I'd say that that quality certainly is not present today. Another thing is that I think musically, in terms of Biggs' music, one of the remarkable things about his music, even when he's playing those solos in the Whiteman Orchestra, is that they are, they have so little of the quality of datedness, to my mind. They're so, they're so fresh and new.
